'''''Heliconius melpomene''''', the '''postman butterfly''', '''common postman''' or simply '''postman''', is a brightly colored, geographically variable butterfly species found throughout [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]]. It was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1758 [[10th edition of Systema Naturae|10th edition of ''Systema Naturae'']]. Its coloration coevolved with another member of the genus, ''[[Heliconius erato|H. erato]]'', as a warning to predators of its inedibility; this is an example of [[Müllerian mimicry]].<ref name="Giraldo-2008">{{cite journal|last1=Giraldo |first1=Nathalia |last2=Salazar |first2=Camilo |last3=Jiggins |first3=Chris D. |last4=Bermingham |first4=Eldredge |last5=Linares |first5=Mauricio |date=28 November 2008 |title=Two sisters in the same dress: ''Heliconius'' cryptic species |journal=BMC Evolutionary Biology |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=324 |doi=10.1186/1471-2148-8-324 |pmid=19040737 |pmc=2632674 |issn=1471-2148 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2008BMCEE...8..324G }}</ref> ''H. melpomene'' was one of the first butterfly species observed to forage for pollen, a behavior that is common in other insect groups but rare in butterflies.<ref name="Gilbert-2017">{{Cite journal |last=Gilbert |first=Lawrence |date=September 2017 |title=Pollen feeding and reproductive biology of ''Heliconius'' butterflies |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=69 |issue=6 |pages=1403–1407 |doi=10.1073/pnas.69.6.1403|pmid=16591992 |pmc=426712 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1972PNAS...69.1403G }}</ref> Because of the recent rapid [[evolutionary radiation]] of the genus ''Heliconius'' and overlapping of its habitat with other related species, ''H. melpomene'' has been the subject of extensive study on [[speciation]] and [[Hybridization (biology)|hybridization]]. These hybrids tend to have low fitness as they look different from the original species and no longer exhibit Müllerian mimicry.

''Heliconius melpomene'' possesses [[ultraviolet]] vision which enhances its ability to distinguish subtle differences between markings on the wings of other butterflies.<ref name="Briscoe-2017">{{Cite journal |last=Briscoe |first=Adriana |date=September 2017 |title=Positive selection of a duplicated UV-sensitive visual pigment coincides with wing pigment evolution in ''Heliconius'' butterflies |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=8 |pages=3628–3633 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0910085107|pmid=20133601 |pmc=2840532 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This allows the butterfly to avoid mating with other species that share the same geographic range.

==Description==
The postman butterfly is predominately black with either red or yellow bands across the [[Insect wing|forewings]]. The postman butterfly has large long wings (35–39 mm). It is poisonous, and the red patterns on its wings are an example of [[aposematism]]. They look similar to ''[[Heliconius erato|H. erato]]''. Two features found on the underside of the hind wings help to distinguish ''H. erato'' from ''H. melpomene''—''H. erato'' usually has four red dots where the wing attaches to the thorax while ''H. melpomene'' usually has three.  In Mexico, Central America and the west coast of Colombia and Ecuador, the yellowish-white stripe on the underside reaches the margin of the hindwing in ''H. erato'' but ends before reaching the margin in ''H. melpomene''.<ref name="Henderson-2010" /><ref name="Tree of Life">{{Cite web|url=http://tolweb.org/Heliconius_melpomene/72252 |title=''Heliconius melpomene'' |website=Tree of Life Web Project |access-date=6 October 2017}}</ref>

There are many geographical races/subspecies/[[Polymorphism (biology)|morphs]] of this butterfly throughout [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cuthill | first1 = J. H. | last2 = Charleston | first2 = M. | year = 2012 | title = Phylogenetic codivergence supports coevolution of mimetic ''Heliconius'' butterflies | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 7 | issue = 5| page = e36464 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0036464| pmid = 22586474 | pmc = 3346731 | bibcode = 2012PLoSO...736464H | doi-access = free }}</ref> The geographical variation in patterns has been studied using [[linkage mapping]] and it has been found that the patterns are associated with a small number of genetic [[locus (genetics)|loci]] called genomic "[[Recombination hotspot|hotspots]]".<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Papa | first1 = R. | last2 = Martin | first2 = A. | last3 = Reed | first3 = R. D. | year = 2008 | title = Genomic hotspots of adaptation in butterfly wing pattern evolution | journal = Current Opinion in Genetics & Development | volume = 18 | issue = 6| pages = 559–564 | doi=10.1016/j.gde.2008.11.007| pmid = 19135357 | s2cid = 205002587 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sheppard | first1 = PM | last2 = Turner | first2 = JRG | last3 = Brown | first3 = KS | last4 = Benson | first4 = WW | last5 = Singer | first5 = MC | year = 1985 | title = Genetics and the evolution of Muellerian mimicry in ''Heliconius'' butterflies | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B | volume = 308 | issue = 1137| pages = 433–613 | doi=10.1098/rstb.1985.0066| bibcode = 1985RSPTB.308..433S | doi-access =  }}</ref> Hotspot loci for color patterning have been found homologous between co-mimics ''H. erato'' and ''H. melpomene'', strengthening evidence for [[parallel evolution]] between the two species, across morph patterns.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Baxter | first1 = S. W. | last2 = Papa | first2 = R. | last3 = Chamberlain | first3 = N. | last4 = Humphray | first4 = S. J. | last5 = Joron | first5 = M. | last6 = Morrison | first6 = C. | last7 = McMillan | first7 = W. O. | last8 = Jiggins | first8 = C. D. | year = 2008 | title = Convergent evolution in the genetic basis of Mullerian mimicry in ''Heliconius'' butterflies | journal = Genetics | volume = 180 | issue = 3| pages = 1567–1577 | doi=10.1534/genetics.107.082982| pmid = 18791259 | pmc = 2581958 }}</ref><ref>Counterman, B. A., F. Araujo-Perez, H. M. Hines, S. W. Baxter, C. M. Morrison, D. P. Lindstrom, R. Papa, L. Ferguson, M. Joron, R. H. Ffrench-Constant, C. P. Smith, D. M. Nielsen, R. Chen, C. D. Jiggins, R. D. Reed, G. Halder, J. Mallet, and W. O. McMillan (2010). "Genomic Hotspots for Adaptation: The Population Genetics of Mullerian Mimicry in ''Heliconius erato''". ''PLOS Genetics'' 6.</ref>

==Geographic range and habitat==
''Heliconius melpomene'' is found from [[Central America]] to [[South America]], especially on the slopes of the [[Andes]] mountains. It most commonly inhabits open terrain and forest edges, although it can also be found near the edges of rivers and streams.<ref name="Henderson-2010">{{Cite book |title=Butterflies, Moths, and Other Invertebrates in Costa Rica |last=Henderson |first=C.L. |publisher=University of Texas Press |year= 2010 |isbn=978-0292719668 |pages=47}}</ref><ref name="Tree of Life" /> It shares its range with other ''Heliconius'' species, and ''H. melpomene'' is usually less abundant than other species.<ref name="Tree of Life" />

==Origins==
A recent study, using [[amplified fragment length polymorphism]] (AFLP) and [[mitochondrial DNA]] datasets, places the origin of ''H. melpomene'' to 2.1 million years ago.<ref name="Quek-2010">{{cite journal | last1 = Quek | first1 = S.P. | last2 = Counterman | first2 = B.A. | last3 = de Moura | first3 = P.A. | last4 = Cardoso | first4 = M.Z. | last5 = Marshall | first5 = C.R. | last6 = McMillan | first6 = W.O. | last7 = Kronforst | first7 = M.R. | year = 2010 | title = Dissecting comimetic radiations in ''Heliconius'' reveals divergent histories of convergent butterflies | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 107 | issue = 16| pages = 7365–7370 | doi=10.1073/pnas.0911572107| pmid = 20368448 | pmc = 2867687 | bibcode = 2010PNAS..107.7365Q | doi-access = free }}</ref> ''H. melpomene'' shows clustering of AFLPs by geography suggesting that the species originated in eastern South America.<ref name="Quek-2010" />

==Food resources==

===Caterpillars===
Caterpillars of ''Heliconius'' exhibit a behavior known as [[monophagy]],<ref name="Smiley-2017">{{Cite journal|last=Smiley |first=John |date=September 2017 |title=Plant chemistry and the evolution of host specificity: new evidence from ''Heliconius'' and ''Passiflora'' |url=http://johnterahsmiley.com/heliconius-passiflora-flea%20beetle/pdfs/sci_78.pdf |journal=Science |volume=201 |issue=4357 |pages=745–747 |doi=10.1126/science.201.4357.745|pmid=17750235 |bibcode=1978Sci...201..745S |s2cid=35030853 }}</ref> meaning they feed on only one kind of plant, specifically the genus ''[[Passiflora]]''. In ''H. melpomene'', the host plants are limited to ''[[Passiflora oerstedii]]'' and ''[[Passiflora menispermifolia]]''. Species of the genus ''Passiflora'' have evolved many chemical defenses, but ''Heliconius'' caterpillars have developed adaptations that allow them to continue to feed on the plants and actually incorporate the toxic compounds into their systems and make them unpalatable to predators. These interactions make ''Heliconius'' and ''Passiflora'' a [[Model organism|model system]] for studies of [[coevolution]].<ref name="de Castro-2018">{{Cite journal |last=de Castro |first=Érika CP |title=The arms race between heliconiine butterflies and ''Passiflora'' plants–new insights on an ancient subject |journal=Biological Reviews |pages= 555–573|doi=10.1111/brv.12357 |pmid=28901723 |volume=93|issue=1 |year=2018 |s2cid=23953807 }}</ref>

===Adults===

====Diet====
Unlike most other butterflies, several ''Heliconius'' species have been observed eating [[pollen]] as well as [[nectar]].<ref name="Gilbert-2017" /> The exact mechanism by which the butterfly digests the pollen is uncertain; it was originally thought that once the pollen was soaked in nectar after ingestion, it would then be able to be digested by the butterfly. Recently, however, the [[enzyme]] [[protease]] was discovered in the butterfly's saliva, which implies an adaptation for breaking down pollen.<ref name="Eberhard-2007">{{Cite journal|last1=Eberhard|first1=S.H.|last2=Hrassnigg|first2=N.|last3=Crailsheim|first3=K.|last4=Krenn|first4=H.W.|date=February 2007|title=Evidence of protease in the saliva of the butterfly ''Heliconius melpomene'' (L.) (Nymphalidae, Lepidoptera)|journal=Journal of Insect Physiology|volume=53|issue=2|pages=126–131|doi=10.1016/j.jinsphys.2006.11.001|issn=0022-1910|pmc=4412925|pmid=17210163|bibcode=2007JInsP..53..126E }}</ref> This enzyme was found in higher concentrations in the saliva of female butterflies, likely due to the greater need of nutrition associated with reproduction.<ref name="Eberhard-2007" /> These adaptations allow the butterflies to extract important [[amino acid]]s from the pollen, which, in addition to general nutrition benefits, allows ''H. melpomene'' to have brighter colors and be more distasteful to predators than their non-pollen-foraging counterparts. It is thought that this foraging adaptation and subsequent enhancement of coloration contributed to the speciation of ''Heliconius''.<ref name="Gilbert-2017" />

====Pollination====
Pollen is a rarely utilized but efficient protein source for ''Lepidoptera'' species. While [[foraging]] for pollen, adults accumulate pollen on the end of their [[proboscis]] and the grains stay there for long periods of time.<ref name="Jiggins-2017a">{{Cite journal |last=Jiggins |first=CD |date=September 2017 |title=Patterns of pollen feeding and habitat preference among ''Heliconius'' species |journal= Ecological Entomology |pages= 448–456|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2311.2002.00434.x |volume=27|issue=4 |s2cid=84938497 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2002EcoEn..27..448E }}</ref> These pollen grains are transferred to the stamen of another plant the butterfly visits while foraging. While there are many plants in ''H. melpomene''{{'s}} range that provide suitable nutrients, only a few of these are visited by the butterfly.<ref name="de Castro-2018" /> This makes the butterfly an efficient pollinator for the flowers it visits as there is a low likelihood of a plant receiving the wrong kind of pollen.<ref name="Jiggins-2017a" />

==Parental care==
By foraging for pollen while developing eggs, female ''H. melpomene'' butterflies provide valuable amino acids and proteins to their offspring. This reduces the amount of time that the offspring must spend foraging during the larval stage, and thus decreases the chances of larval predation.<ref name="Gilbert-2017" /> While this extra foraging behavior on the part of the female increases her likelihood of being eaten, the warning colors highlighting her distaste protect her from would be predators.<ref name="Gilbert-2017" />

===Oviposition===
Female ''H. melpomene'' butterflies recognize host plants by identifying the corresponding chemical compound using [[chemoreceptor]]s located on her forelegs. When searching for a plant, the butterfly will drum her legs on the plant in order to detect the chemical compounds the plant releases. Once she has found the correct host plant, she will lay eggs singly on separate young leaves.<ref name="Briscoe-2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Briscoe |first1=Adriana D. |last2=Macias-Muñoz |first2=Aide |last3=Kozak |first3=Krzysztof M. |last4=Walters |first4=James R. |last5=Yuan |first5=Furong |last6=Jamie |first6=Gabriel A. |last7=Martin |first7=Simon H. |last8=Dasmahapatra |first8=Kanchon K. |last9=Ferguson |first9=Laura C. |date=11 July 2013 |title=Female Behaviour Drives Expression and Evolution of Gustatory Receptors in Butterflies |journal=PLOS Genetics |volume=9 |issue=7 |pages=e1003620 |doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1003620 |pmid=23950722 |pmc=3732137 |issn=1553-7404 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Finding the correct host plant is crucial as ''H. melpomene'' larvae are adapted to only feed on certain ''Passiflora'' plants.<ref name="Smiley-2017" />

==Life cycle==
The eggs of ''H. melpomene'' are yellow and approximately 1.5 x 1 mm.<ref name="Tree of Life" /> They are mostly laid singly or rarely in small clusters on the young leaves of ''Passiflora'' plants. Caterpillars live in groups of two to three individuals and are white with black spots.<ref name="Tree of Life" /> Pupae are spiny and dark brown in color.<ref name="Tree of Life" /> The adults have black bodies with bright yellow or orange patterns on the wings.<ref name="Jiggins-2017b">{{Cite web|url=http://tolweb.org/Heliconius_melpomene/72252|title=Heliconius melpomene|last=Jiggins|first=Chris|date=November 2017|website=The Tree of Life Web Project}}</ref> Female ''H. melpomene'' produce oocytes continuously throughout their life; this is due to the high nutrient diet the butterfly obtains from eating pollen.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dunlap-Pianka|first1=Helen|last2=Boggs|first2=Carol L.|last3=Gilbert|first3=Lawrence E.|date=1977-07-29|title=Ovarian Dynamics in Heliconiine Butterflies: Programmed Senescence versus Eternal Youth|journal=Science|language=en|volume=197|issue=4302|pages=487–490|doi=10.1126/science.197.4302.487|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17783249|bibcode=1977Sci...197..487D|s2cid=46098536}}</ref> Closely related ''Heliconius'' species have been reported to have a maximum life span of six months, and it is likely that ''H. melpomene'' lives for a similar length of time.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ehrlich|first=Paul|date=November 2017|title=Population Structure and Dynamics of the Tropical Butterfly Heliconius Ethilla|journal=Biotropica|volume=5|issue=2|pages=69–82|doi=10.2307/2989656|jstor=2989656|bibcode=1973Biotr...5...69E }}</ref>

==Protective coloration and behavior==

===Mimicry===
''Heliconius melpomene'' coevolved with its sister species, ''[[Heliconius erato|H. erato]]'', each developing similar bright color patterns.<ref name="Giraldo-2008" /> The ''H. melpomene'' patterns correspond to at least 20 of the 27 ''H. erato'' subspecies.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gilbert|first=Lawrence E.|date=1972|title=Pollen Feeding and Reproductive Biology of ''Heliconius'' Butterflies|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=69|issue=6|pages=1403–1407|doi=10.1073/pnas.69.6.1403|pmid=16591992|jstor=61399|pmc=426712|bibcode=1972PNAS...69.1403G|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brower|first=Andrew V. Z.|date=1994|title=Rapid Morphological Radiation and Convergence Among Races of the Butterfly ''Heliconius erato'' Inferred from Patterns of Mitochondrial DNA Evolution|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=91|issue=14|pages=6491–6495|doi=10.1073/pnas.91.14.6491|jstor=2364999|pmc=44228|pmid=8022810|bibcode=1994PNAS...91.6491B|doi-access=free}}</ref> This coloration warns potential predators that the butterflies are distasteful and should be avoided; this is an example of [[aposematism]]. Since both species possess this acrid taste, they display what is known as [[Müllerian mimicry]]. Despite their easily confused coloration, these two species are able to exist in the same habitat range because they are [[reproductively isolated]] due to adaptations in the eyes of the butterflies that allow for better distinction between individuals.<ref name="Giraldo-2008" />

===Chemical defense===
Both males and females release a strong odor detectable even to humans when handled in order to deter predation. Additionally, ''H. melpomene'' butterflies render themselves unpalatable to predators such as birds by producing [[Glycoside|cyanogenic glycosides]] in both the larval and adult stages.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nahrstedt |first1=A. |last2=Davis |first2=R. H. |date=1 January 1983 |title=Occurrence, variation and biosynthesis of the cyanogenic glucosides linamarin and lotaustralin in species of the Heliconiini (Insecta: Lepidoptera) |journal=Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part B: Comparative Biochemistry |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=65–73 |doi=10.1016/0305-0491(83)90041-X}}</ref> These glycosides are incorporated into the insect's system by feeding on host plants that produce the compounds as a defense against herbivory.

===Communal roosting===
Individuals of the genus ''Heliconius'' form large [[Communal roosting|communal roosts]] which they return to each night after foraging.<ref name="Finkbeiner-2012">{{Cite journal|last1=Finkbeiner|first1=Susan D.|last2=Briscoe|first2=Adriana D.|last3=Reed|first3=Robert D.|date=22 July 2012|title=The benefit of being a social butterfly: communal roosting deters predation|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=279 |issue=1739 |pages=2769–2776 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2012.0203 |issn=0962-8452|pmid=22438492 |pmc=3367783}}</ref> The reason for this behavior was not well characterized until recently when it was determined that the large aggregations of butterflies provided protection from predators. Butterflies fare better in these groups for two reasons. First, the prey dilution effect lowers the likelihood that one particular individual will be eaten because of the large number of other individuals that are in the area. Second, the congregation of the brightly colored individuals is more likely to deter predators by making the warning coloration more prominent.<ref name="Finkbeiner-2012" />

==Genetics==

===Hybridization===
Due to its overlapping range with many closely related species, ''H. melpomene'' sometimes [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridizes]] in nature despite adaptations meant to counteract this.<ref name="ProQuest">{{Cite web|url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/01da7d4c8a138e7c95f678073b2baaff/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=40569|title=Reproductive isolation caused by colour pattern mimicry|website=ProQuest|language=en|access-date=3 October 2017}}</ref> Females resulting from the cross of ''H. melpomene'' and ''[[Heliconius cydno|H. cydno]]'' are sterile. While hybrid males are not sterile, they exhibit patterns that are intermediate between the crossed species and thus the males are unlikely to be recognized as mates by either species. Furthermore, the patterns on both sexes will be non-mimetic, meaning they will not be recognized by predators as displays of distaste. Therefore, the hybrids resulting from the cross of ''H. melpomene'' with other ''Heliconius'' species have low fitness and are not likely to persist.<ref name="ProQuest"/>

===Hybrid speciation===
Hybridisation of ''Heliconius melpomene'' with ''[[Heliconius pardalinus]]'' resulted in the hybrid speciation of ''[[Heliconius elevatus]]''.<ref name="Liebniz-2024">A new butterfly species was created by two species hybridising 200,000 years ago. (2024, April 17). Leibniz Institute for the Analysis of Biodiversity Change (LIB). Retrieved April 21, 2024, from https://leibniz-lib.de/en/2024-04-17-new-butterfly-species/</ref><ref name="Rosser-2024">Rosser, N., Seixas, F., Queste, L.M. et al. Hybrid speciation driven by multilocus introgression of ecological traits. Nature (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07263-w</ref>

==Mating==

===Mate searching===
When searching for mates, males of ''H. melpomene'' exhibit patrolling behavior, which involves searching for potential mates while flying around the range that the species inhabits.<ref name="ProQuest" /> This requires the ability to distinguish ''H. melpomene'' females from those of other species, a key adaptation of the butterfly.

===Female/male interactions===
Male ''H. melpomene'' possess abdominal [[clasper]]s that are used to grasp females for forced copulations.<ref name="Schulz-2008">{{Cite journal|last1=Schulz|first1=Stefan|last2=Estrada|first2=Catalina|last3=Yildizhan|first3=Selma|last4=Boppré|first4=Michael|last5=Gilbert|first5=Lawrence E.|date=1 January 2008|title=An Antiaphrodisiac in ''Heliconius melpomene'' Butterflies|journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology|language=en|volume=34|issue=1|pages=82–93|doi=10.1007/s10886-007-9393-z|pmid=18080165|bibcode=2008JCEco..34...82S |s2cid=22090974|issn=0098-0331}}</ref> During mating, the male passes nutrients in a [[spermatophore]]; the female can use this [[nuptial gift]] to nourish the fertilizing eggs inside her. In addition to the spermatophore, males also deliver a [[pheromone]] to the female that is an [[antiaphrodisiac]] to other males. This increases the likelihood of the male's reproductive success by preventing the female from mating with any other males, which ensures that only the original male's sperm will be used to fertilize the female's eggs.. The pheromone is produced only by males and is secreted to identify themselves to other males, so the antiaphrodisiac works by making the female smell like a male.<ref name="Schulz-2008"/> After a period of time the pheromone wears off and the female is able to mate again, which she will do several times throughout her life.<ref name="Jiggins-2017b" />

==Physiology==

===Vision===
Due to a duplication in a gene for UV light detection, ''H. melpomene'' individuals are capable of distinguishing between a wider range of yellow shades than other butterfly species.<ref name="Briscoe-2017" /> Additionally, when looking for mates, the butterflies distinguish conspecifics from hybrids and heterospecifics by detecting subtle changes in marking patterns on wings. These adaptations allow the butterflies to avoid genetically costly mates, as hybrid females are sterile and hybrid males in this system are less fit due to [[disruptive selection|disruptive sexual selection]].<ref name="Briscoe-2017" />

===Gustation/tasting===
While both sexes of ''H. melpomene'' possess [[taste receptor]]s on their hindlegs, only the female butterflies have the receptors on the forelegs; this is an example of [[sexual dimorphism]]. The taste receptors are used by both sexes in order to find food and mates, but the female also uses the sense to find suitable host plants for her eggs.<ref name="Briscoe-2013" /> These taste receptors are highly specialized due to the coevolution with the ''Passiflora'' plant.
